short_definition: Bootstrapping is building and growing a business using personal savings and the company's own revenue instead of raising outside investment from venture capitalists or other equity investors.
explanation: Bootstrapping means the business grows on money it earns rather than money raised from investors. Bootstrapped founders typically start small, keep costs low, charge customers early and reinvest profits to fund growth. Some bridge gaps with modest loans or side income such as freelancing, but they avoid selling ownership stakes.

Founders who bootstrap keep full ownership and control. The business is pushed to find paying customers and sustainable economics early, without investor pressure to chase rapid growth or a quick exit.

The trade-off is speed and personal risk. Growth is usually slower and limited by cash flow, and well-funded competitors may move faster. Founders often put their own savings at stake or go without a salary. Personal guarantees on business loans can also put personal assets at risk. Set a clear limit on how much of your own money you will put in, and track your cash runway.
example: Illustrative example: A founder starts an online course business with $3,000 of savings for software and a website. In the first month, sales bring in $1,500. She spends $500 on running costs and reinvests $1,000 in ads and better recording equipment. By keeping expenses below revenue each month, she grows without giving up any ownership, but her growth is limited to what sales can fund.
common_mistake: Funding the business with all personal savings or high-interest credit cards and no limit on how much to lose. This puts personal finances and the emergency fund at risk.
title: Bootstrapping
